title: Introduction to Bit Manipulation
description: Understand bits, binary numbers, and basic bitwise operations like AND, OR, XOR, and shifts

sections.title: 5. 10 most important bit manipulation patterns

blocks.text: Every integer stored in a computer is represented as a sequence of binary digits (bits), where each bit can be either 0 or 1. Bit manipulation is the technique of directly accessing and modifying these individual bits using specialized operations such as AND, OR, XOR, NOT, and bit shifts.

By working at the binary level, bit manipulation enables highly efficient solutions for many programming problems, including optimization, state representation, mathematical computations, and low-level system operations.
Computers store numbers using bits. In an 8-bit representation, each position corresponds to a power of 2:
Each bit contributes its value only if it is 1. Therefore:
Notice that each position is worth twice the value of the position to its right, which is why binary is called a base-2 number system.
Understanding this representation is the foundation of bit manipulation, since all bitwise operations work directly on these individual 0s and 1s.
Bit manipulation is one of the most powerful tools in a programmer's toolkit because it allows you to work directly with the binary representation of data.

items: Extremely fast: Most bitwise operations are executed in a single CPU instruction, making them among the fastest operations available.
Memory efficient: Problems that seem to require extra arrays, sets, or hash maps can often be solved using a few bits, reducing space complexity from O(n) to O(1).
Common in interviews: Bit manipulation frequently appears in coding interviews, especially in problems involving unique elements, subsets, state compression, and optimization.
Widely used in systems: Operating systems, databases, networking protocols, cryptography, and game engines all rely heavily on bit-level operations.

blocks.text: Mastering bit manipulation not only helps you solve interview problems but also deepens your understanding of how computers actually work.
Computers typically represent negative integers using a system called Two's Complement.
To convert a positive number to its negative representation:

items: Flip all bits (0 → 1, 1 → 0)
Add 1 to the result

blocks.text: Computers cannot store a minus sign (-) directly, so they use a special representation called Two's Complement to store negative numbers.
To get the negative version of a number, the computer flips all its bits (0 → 1, 1 → 0) and then adds 1.

For example, to represent -5, it starts with the binary form of 5, flips all the bits, and adds 1. This representation makes arithmetic operations like addition and subtraction much simpler for the CPU.
A useful consequence of Two's Complement is that the bitwise NOT operator (~) follows the formula ~n = -(n + 1).
For example, ~5 = -6. Another interesting fact is that -1 is represented by all bits being 1. In an 8-bit system, -1 is stored as 11111111.
Understanding Two's Complement helps explain why bitwise operations behave the way they do when working with negative numbers.
Simple: How negative numbers are stored. To negate a number: flip all bits, then add 1. This is why~n = -(n + 1)always holds. The number -1 is stored as11111111in 8-bit.
These six operators are the building blocks of every bit trick. Learn the truth table for each that single table tells you everything about its behaviour.
Output is 1 only whenbothbits are 1. Think of it as "both switches must be ON". Primary use: masking  zero out specific bits while keeping others intact.
The AND (&) operator compares two bits and returns 1 only when both bits are 1. In every other case, the result is 0. That's what the truth table in the image shows.

When both A and B are 0, the result is 0. When one is 0 and the other is 1, the result is still 0. Only when both A and B are 1 does the result become 1. You can think of AND as asking: "Are both values 1?"If the answer is yes, return 1; otherwise, return 0.
Now let's apply this to the numbers 9 and 6.

items: Step 1: First, convert both numbers into binary form. The number 9 becomes 1001 and 6 becomes 0110.
Step 2: The AND (&) operator compares the bits at the same positions in both numbers. It returns 1 only if both bits are 1; otherwise, it returns 0.
Step 3: Compare each position one by one. In every position, either one bit is 0 or both are not 1 together, so each comparison produces 0.
Step 4: After comparing all positions, the resulting binary number is 0000.
Step 5: Convert 0000 back to decimal. It equals 0.

blocks.text: Intuition: The AND operator keeps only the common 1s between two numbers. Since 9 (1001) and 6 (0110) don't have a single position where both contain 1, no bits survive, and the answer becomes 0.
Output is 1 whenat least onebit is 1. Primary use: setting bits force a specific position to 1 without touching the others.

For the numbers 9 and 6, the binary representations are 1001 and 0110. When OR compares each position, every position contains at least one 1, so every position in the result becomes 1. The final result is 1111, which is 15 in decimal. Therefore, 9 | 6 = 15.

items: Step 1: Convert both numbers into their binary representations.
Step 2: Compare the bits at the same positions using the OR operator.
Step 3: For each position, if at least one of the two bits is 1, put 1 in the result. Only if both bits are 0 do you put 0.
Step 4: After comparing all positions, combine the resulting bits to form the final binary number.
Step 5: Convert the final binary number back to decimal to get the answer.

blocks.text: Intuition: Think of OR as combining all the 1s from both numbers. Any position that contains a 1 in either number will also contain a 1 in the result. That's why OR is often used when you want to turn bits on or merge information from multiple bit patterns.

Output is 1 only when the two bitsdiffer. Key properties:a ^ a = 0anda ^ 0 = a. XOR is self-cancelling apply it twice and you get back the original. Uses: toggling bits, finding unique elements, no-temp swaps.
For example, consider the numbers 9 and 6. In binary, 9 = 1001 and 6 = 0110. When XOR compares the bits position by position, every pair of bits is different.
Because all comparisons are different, every position in the result becomes 1. The final result is 1111, which is 15 in decimal. Therefore, 9 ^ 6 = 15.

items: Step 1: Convert both numbers into their binary representations.
Step 2: Compare the bits at the same positions using the XOR operator.
Step 3: For each position, put 1 if the two bits are different. If the two bits are the same, put 0.
Step 4: After comparing all positions, combine the resulting bits to form the final binary number.
Step 5: Convert the final binary number back to decimal to get the answer.

blocks.text: Intuition: Think of XOR as keeping only the differences between two numbers. Wherever the bits are different, XOR produces 1. Wherever they are the same, XOR produces 0. This is why XOR is often used to find unique elements, toggle bits, and detect differences between values.
Flips every single bit 0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0. In two's complement,~n = -(n + 1). Used to build inverted masks, e.g.~(1<<k)gives a mask with 0 only at position k and 1s everywhere else.

For example, the number 9 is represented as 1001 (shown in the image). After applying the NOT operator, all bits are flipped, giving 0110. However, computers store negative numbers using Two's Complement, so the result is interpreted as -10, not 6.

items: Step 1: Take the binary representation of the number.
Step 2: Apply the NOT (~) operator.
Step 3: Flip every bit change all 1s to 0s and all 0s to 1s.
Step 4: The resulting bit pattern is interpreted using Two's Complement representation.
Step 5: The final value becomes -(n + 1).
So, for the number 9, the result of applying NOT is -10.

blocks.text: Intuition: Think of NOT as reversing every bit in the number. Because computers use Two's Complement for negative numbers, the flipped result ends up representing the negative of the next number, which is why ~9 = -10 and, in general, ~n = -(n + 1).
Moves every bit left by k positions. Rightmost positions fill with 0, leftmost bits fall off. Formula:n << k = n × 2^k. Each left shift by 1 doubles the value the fastest possible multiply.
The Left Shift (<<) operator moves all bits to the left by a specified number of positions. Every time you shift left by 1 position, the number gets multiplied by 2.
Shifting left by 2 positions multiplies the number by 4, shifting by 3 positionsmultiplies it by 8, and so on.
In the image, the number 6 is shifted left by 2 positions. Moving all bits two places to the left adds two zeros at the end, which makes the value four times larger. As a result, 6 becomes 24.

items: Step 1: Take the binary representation of the number.
Step 2: Move every bit to the left by the specified number of positions.
Step 3: Fill the empty positions on the right with 0s.
Step 4: The new binary number now represents a larger value.
Step 5: Convert the result back to decimal to get the final answer.

blocks.text: Intuition: Think of a left shift as multiplying by powers of 2. If you shift left by k positions, the number becomes number × 2ᵏ. That's why 6 << 2 = 6 × 4 = 24.

The Right Shift (>>) operator moves all bits to the right by a specified number of positions. Every time you shift right by 1 position, the number gets divided by 2 (ignoring any remainder). Shifting right by 2 positions divides the number by 4, shifting by 3 positions divides it by 8, and so on.
In the image, the number 24 is shifted right by 2 positions. Moving all bits two places to the right removes the last two bits, making the value four times smaller. As a result, 24 becomes 6.

items: Step 1: Take the binary representation of the number.
Step 2: Move every bit to the right by the specified number of positions.
Step 3: Fill the empty positions on the left with 0s (for positive numbers).
Step 4: The new binary number now represents a smaller value.
Step 5: Convert the result back to decimal to get the final answer.

blocks.text: Intuition: Think of a right shift as dividing by powers of 2. If you shift right by k positions, the number becomes number ÷ 2ᵏ (for positive integers). That's why 24 >> 2 = 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

content.title: 5. 10 most important bit manipulation patterns

blocks.text: These are the exact patterns that appear over and over in DSA problems. Master these and you can solve a wide range of interview questions in O(1) time and space.
1. Check if the k-th Bit is Set
This pattern is used when you want to know whether a particular bit in a number is 1 or 0.
It is one of the most common bit operations because many bit manipulation problems require reading a specific bit.
We shift the number right until the target bit reaches the last position.
Then we check that last bit.

If it is 1, the bit is set.
If it is 0, the bit is not set.
This pattern is used when you want to force a specific bit to become 1.
If the bit is already 1, nothing changes.
We create a mask containing a 1 only at the target position.
Using OR (|) guarantees that position becomes 1.
This pattern is used when you want to force a specific bit to become 0.
We create a mask that has 0 only at the target position and 1 everywhere else.
AND (&) with that mask removes only the desired bit.

items: If the bit is 0, it becomes 1
If the bit is 1, it becomes 0

blocks.text: XOR (^) flips bits wherever the mask contains a 1.
Since the mask contains a 1 only at the target position, only that bit changes.
This pattern determines whether a number is odd or even.
It is one of the simplest and fastest bit tricks.
The last bit tells us everything.

items: Last bit = 1 → Odd
Last bit = 0 → Even

6. Check if a Number is a Power of 2
This pattern checks whether a number is a power of 2.
A power of 2 always has exactly one set bit in its binary representation.
When we subtract 1 from it, that set bit becomes 0 and all bits to its right become 1.
ANDing these two numbers always gives 0.
Result is 0, so 8 is a power of 2.
This pattern counts how many 1s are present in the binary representation of a number.
This is also called the Population Count or Hamming Weight.
If we keep doing this until the number becomes 0, the number of operations performed equals the number of set bits.
Remove the rightmost set bit repeatedly:
This pattern finds the value of the rightmost set bit.
It is commonly used in Fenwick Trees and advanced bit manipulation problems.
removes every bit except the lowest set bit.
The result contains only that bit.
Therefore, the lowest set bit has value 4.
9. Find the Unique Element Using XOR
This pattern finds the element that appears exactly once when every other element appears twice.
This is one of the most famous XOR interview problems.
So whenever two equal numbers are XORed together, they cancel out.
After XORing the entire array, only the unique element remains.
This pattern swaps two numbers without using an extra variable.
It is a classic bit manipulation trick.
When the same value is XORed twice, it cancels itself out.
Using three XOR operations, the values of two variables can be exchanged.
The values have been swapped without using a temporary variable.
Although this trick is interesting, modern code usually uses a temporary variable because it is easier to read and less error-prone.

A 32-bit integer can represent any subset of a 32-element set. Bit i = 1 means element i is in the set. Every subset operation becomes a single CPU instruction far faster than a HashSet for small universes (up to ~20 elements).
This pattern is called Bitmask DP and it solves problems like: Travelling Salesman, minimum team covering all skills, shortest superstring.
This operation adds element i to the set by turning its bit to 1. If the element is already present, nothing changes.

This operation removes element i from the set by turning its bit to 0. All other bits remain unchanged.
3. Check if an Element Exists ((mask >> i) & 1)
This operation checks whether element i is present in the set. If the result is 1, the element exists; otherwise, it does not.
This operation counts how many elements are currently in the set by counting the number of 1s in the bitmask.
5. Union of Two Sets (A ∪ B or mask1 | mask2)
The union contains every element that appears in either set.
6. Intersection of Two Sets (A ∩ B or mask1 & mask2)
The intersection contains only the elements that appear in both sets.
The difference contains elements that are present in A but not in B.
This technique generates every possible subset of a set represented by a bitmask.
For a set with k elements, there are exactly 2ᵏ subsets, so this loop visits each subset once
